title: Judah Halevi
hookLine: poet who wrote that his heart was in the east while he lived at the end of the west

lines: A POET WHOSE HEART FACED EAST.
cards: A phone sits on a kitchen table in one city, open to the weather in another. Some people keep an app like that: the forecast for where their parents were born, or where someone they love lives now.
They check it without thinking. Rain there. Sun there.

The body is here, and part of the attention is always there. A poet in medieval Spain put something like that split into a short Hebrew poem. Today, Judah Halevi, the poet of the heart that faced east.

teach.b: Judah Halevi lived in Christian and Muslim Spain: a doctor by trade, a celebrated poet, with friends, students and a comfortable life. And yet one short poem of his opens with a split.

teach.h: MY HEART IS IN THE EAST.
teach.b: Put plainly: my heart is in the east, and I am at the far end of the west. East is Jerusalem, the land of Israel. West is Spain, the edge of the map as he knew it.

He asks how he can taste food or enjoy anything while Zion is in other hands and he is far away. Leaving all the good things of Spain would be easy, he says, if only he could see the dust of the ruined sanctuary.

teach.h: IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.
teach.b: Psalm one hundred thirty-seven, sung by exiles by the rivers of Babylon, says in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning."

Halevi makes that old vow personal and present tense. He also wrote a set of poems to Zion itself, addressing the land like a beloved; some of them are recited on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple's destruction.
Here is what lifts it beyond a poem. He decided to go. His poems describe the sea voyage, the waves, the fear, the ship.
Tradition tells a legend that he reached the gates of Jerusalem, knelt to kiss the ground while reciting his poem to Zion, and was struck down by a passing rider. Nobody can confirm that story.

teach.h: HE DID NOT ONLY LONG. HE WENT.
teach.b: But the poems that survive show a man who did not only long. He packed.

how: Judah Halevi's poems to Zion are part of the kinot, the laments recited on Tisha B'Av in some communities, and his line about the heart in the east is quoted in Jewish writing about the land of Israel.

o: a poet whose heart was in the east, in Zion
the poet of Keter Malchut, read on Yom Kippur
a doctor who stayed content in Spain's courts

p: Spain, the edge of his map
if I forget thee, O Jerusalem
when some recite his poems to Zion

s: Judah Halevi was poor and unhappy in Spain
he was a doctor and celebrated poet with friends and a comfortable life, and still his heart faced east.
the story of his death at the gates of Jerusalem is a legend
tradition tells it, but nobody can confirm it.
the psalm's vow, if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, lies behind his poems.

games.q: you are Judah Halevi: a respected doctor and poet in Spain, comfortable, surrounded by friends. but your heart is in the east. what do you do?
o: keep writing about it from home.
set out on the sea journey east.
games.why: he set out. His poems describe the sea voyage, and a legend says he reached Jerusalem's gates. The poems show he did not only long. He went.

practice: Feel where your body is, the chair, the floor, and then ask gently where your heart is right now: with a person, a place, a worry, a hope. Don't judge it; let it point, and stay with that direction for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can bring that place or person into your prayer in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Judah Halevi. A poet and doctor in Spain who wrote that his heart was in the east, wrote poems to Zion, and set out to go there. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my heart in the east. A longing that ended up as a journey. Day nine hundred twenty-three, done.
